title: Detroit's Black political leadership expands in city government
description: On January 5, 1982, Detroit's newly elected city leadership began another year of Coleman A. Young's administration, with Black elected officials holding a dominant role in municipal government.
significance: Detroit's city government had become one of the nation's most prominent examples of sustained Black electoral power.

title: Detroit's Black political leadership begins Coleman Young's second mayoral term
description: On January 9, 1977, Coleman A. Young began his second term as mayor of Detroit after winning reelection in November 1976.
significance: Young's reelection demonstrated the durability of Black electoral power in Detroit and continued the city's historic period of Black mayoral leadership.

sources.title: Coleman A. Young — Detroit Historical Society

title: Coleman A. Young takes office as Detroit's first Black mayor
description: In January 1974, Coleman A. Young formally began his first term as Detroit's mayor after winning the 1973 election. His administration became a defining period in the city's modern political history.
significance: Young's administration represented a major transfer of political power to Detroit's Black majority and shaped city government for the next two decades.

sources.title: Coleman A. Young — Detroit Historical Society

significance: The movement helped create a permanent institutional infrastructure for documenting Detroit's Black past at a time when many Black neighborhoods, buildings, and records were threatened by redevelopment.

description: In February 1987, Rosa Parks and Elaine Eason Steele co-founded the Rosa and Raymond Parks Institute for Self Development in Detroit, creating an organization dedicated to helping young people develop leadership and civic responsibility.
significance: The institute became one of Parks's most important Detroit legacies, carrying civil-rights education to new generations through programs including Pathways to Freedom.

title: Teola Hunter is born in Detroit
description: Teola Hunter was born in Detroit on February 5, 1933, and grew up on the city's lower east side. She later became an educator, was elected to the Michigan House of Representatives in 1980, and in 1986 became the first African American woman to serve as Michigan House speaker pro tem.
significance: Hunter's career connected Black Detroit's public-school and neighborhood communities to state-level political leadership and marked a major milestone for Black women in Michigan government.

sources.title: Michigan Advance — On this day in 1933: Historic state House member Teola Hunter is born
sources.notes: Documents Hunter's February 5, 1933 Detroit birth, lower east side upbringing, and later political career.

significance: Woodson's Detroit appearances helped connect the city to the national movement to preserve, teach and celebrate African American history, decades before Negro History Month became a national observance.

description: On April 1, 1968, Detroit joined cities across the country in mourning after the assassination of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. The city's Black leadership and civil-rights organizations prepared public memorial activity and demonstrations following King's death in Memphis on March 4.
significance: King had a deep connection to Detroit through the 1963 Walk to Freedom, and his death profoundly affected Detroit's Black community and civil-rights movement.

significance: The opening marked a major expansion of Detroit's leading Black history institution and created one of the world's largest museums devoted to African American history and culture.

title: First Independence National Bank opens in Detroit
description: First Independence National Bank of Detroit opened in May 1970 as part of a Black-led effort to keep financial resources circulating in Detroit's Black community. Dr. Karl Gregory and other Black economic organizers helped establish the institution through the economic-development work of the Inner City Business Improvement Forum.
significance: The bank became a major example of Black economic self-determination in post-uprising Detroit, creating a locally controlled financial institution intended to expand access to capital for Black households and businesses.

title: Detroit's first recorded race riot begins
description: On June 14–15, 1833, Detroit experienced its first recorded race riot after Black Detroiters helped Thornton and Ruth Blackburn, a fugitive slave couple, escape toward Canada. The violence became an important turning point in Detroit's organized antislavery movement.
significance: The episode helped catalyze organized antislavery activity in Detroit and shows how Black Detroiters were directly involved in resistance to slavery and the enforcement of the Fugitive Slave system.

significance: White's career opened a path for Black women in Michigan electoral politics. Her death at age 39 ended a pioneering legislative career rooted in Detroit's Black civic and political community.

title: Library of Congress documents unemployed Black Detroiters
description: On September 14, 1976, photographer Bob Benyas created a series of images in Detroit documenting unemployed Black residents. The Library of Congress finding aid records multiple image jobs from that date.
significance: The images provide a primary-source snapshot of Black Detroit's economic conditions during the city's post-industrial transition.

title: Charles H. Wright's International Afro-American Museum expands its Detroit program
description: In September 1966, Dr. Charles H. Wright's International Afro-American Museum expanded its public programming in Detroit, building on the museum he founded the previous year to preserve African American history and culture.
significance: Wright's museum became a cornerstone of Black historical preservation in Detroit and eventually grew into the Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History.

sources.title: Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History — Detroit Historical Society

title: Damon Keith is confirmed to the U.S. Court of Appeals
description: On October 20, 1977, the U.S. Senate confirmed Detroit-born federal judge Damon Keith to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit. About 700 people later attended his swearing-in ceremony in downtown Detroit.
significance: Keith was a major Detroit civil-rights jurist whose career included landmark rulings on school desegregation, urban renewal, and government surveillance.
organizations: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit

sources.title: On this day in 1977: Damon Keith secures U.S. Court of Appeals seat — Michigan Advance
sources.notes: Documents the October 20, 1977 confirmation and Detroit swearing-in context.

verification.notes: The confirmation occurred in Washington, while the Detroit event was the subsequent swearing-in. Confirm the exact swearing-in date before using this as a Detroit On This Day entry.

title: Lillian Hatcher becomes the UAW's first Black female union representative
description: On October 21, 1944, Detroit resident Lillian Hatcher was appointed to the United Auto Workers' Women's Division of War Policy, becoming the first Black woman to serve as a UAW representative.
significance: Hatcher's appointment marked a major breakthrough for Black women in the Detroit labor movement during World War II and expanded Black women's influence inside organized labor.

sources.title: On this day in 1944: Lillian Hatcher becomes UAW's first Black female union rep — Michigan Advance

title: Detroit Black theater leaders expand the city's cultural institutions
description: On October 25, 1985, Detroit's Black theater community continued building audiences and institutions through locally produced theater and cultural programming.
significance: Black theater was an important part of Detroit's cultural infrastructure, providing space for Black playwrights, actors, directors, and audiences.

title: Brewster housing project dedication
description: On November 2, 1938, a dedication ceremony was held for the Brewster housing project in Detroit. The Detroit Public Library's Burton Historical Collection preserves a photograph of the dedication crowd and identifies the scene as African American Detroit.
significance: Brewster became one of the most important public-housing developments in Black Detroit, making this dedication a useful entry point into the history of housing, migration and community life in the city.

sources.title: Crowd at Brewster housing dedication — Detroit Public Library Digital Collections

title: Carter G. Woodson speaks at Ebenezer A.M.E. Church
description: Carter G. Woodson spoke at Detroit's Ebenezer African Methodist Episcopal Church, continuing his work promoting the study and teaching of African American history.
significance: Woodson's repeated appearances in Detroit demonstrate the city's importance in the early Black history movement and the role of local Black churches as educational and cultural centers.
organizations: Association for the Study of Negro Life and History

title: William T. Patrick Jr. becomes Detroit's first Black city council member since Reconstruction
description: Detroit attorney William T. Patrick Jr. won election to the Detroit Common Council in November 1957, becoming the first African American elected to the council since the 1880s. His victory followed years of Black voter organizing and labor support for greater representation in city government.
significance: Patrick's election marked the return of Black representation to Detroit's city council after roughly seven decades and helped open a new era of Black political power in city government.

sources.title: Michigan State Historic Preservation Office — The Civil Rights Movement and the African American Experience in 20th Century Detroit
sources.notes: Identifies Patrick as the first African American elected to the Detroit Common Council and cites contemporary Detroit Free Press reporting on his 1957 election.

title: Coleman A. Young is elected Detroit's first Black mayor
description: On November 8, 1973, Coleman A. Young won the Detroit mayoral election, defeating Police Commissioner John F. Nichols and becoming Detroit's first Black mayor.
significance: Young's victory transformed Detroit politics and began a 20-year mayoral tenure that reshaped city government, policing, development, and Black political power.

title: Detroit dedicates a Michigan historical marker at Elmwood Cemetery
description: On November 23, 1976, Detroit officials dedicated a Michigan historical marker at Elmwood Cemetery, with Mayor Coleman A. Young and City Councilman Ernest C. Browne Jr. among those present.
significance: The dedication was part of Detroit's 1970s effort to document and preserve historic sites across the city during a period when Black Detroiters were increasingly shaping the city's public historical record.

title: Black Workers Congress is formed in Detroit
description: On December 12, 1970, the Black Workers Congress was formed in Detroit by activists emerging from the League of Revolutionary Black Workers and other Black labor organizations.
significance: The organization reflected Detroit's central role in Black labor organizing and the effort to connect workplace struggles with broader demands for racial and economic justice.

sources.title: Anarchy in Detroit: A Glimpse of the 20th Century — University of Michigan
sources.notes: The University of Michigan timeline dates the formation of the Black Workers Congress in Detroit to December 12, 1970.

title: Jazz guitarist Earl Klugh is born in Detroit
description: Jazz guitarist and composer Earl Klugh was born in Detroit on September 16, 1953. He began playing piano as a child before taking up guitar and developing his career in Detroit's music community.
significance: Klugh became an internationally recognized jazz guitarist and composer, connecting Detroit's musical tradition to the broader history of contemporary jazz.

title: Beulah Whitby gives an oral-history interview about Black Detroit
description: Detroit social worker Beulah Whitby was interviewed on September 16, 1969. The oral-history interview documented her experiences and recollections concerning Black Detroit, including the Depression era, the Sojourner Truth Homes controversy, the 1943 Detroit race riot, the NAACP, the Urban League, and Detroit's Black community.
significance: The interview preserves firsthand historical testimony about Black Detroit from a community leader who had worked with the Detroit Commission on Community Relations.

title: Federal court hears Annie Thompson's case against Chrysler
description: On September 16, 1974, the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan issued an order in Thompson v. Chrysler Corporation involving Annie Thompson, a 55-year-old Black former Chrysler employee seeking relief in connection with her employment claims.
significance: The case provides a window into the intersection of Black women's employment, labor rights, age discrimination, and industrial work in Detroit during the 1970s.
organizations: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan

title: Detroit Commission on Community Relations challenges police investigation after Cobo Hall assault
description: On September 16, 1968, the Detroit Commission on Community Relations criticized the investigation conducted by the Citizen Complaint Bureau into a police assault at Cobo Hall.
significance: The episode reflects continuing concerns about police accountability in Detroit following the 1967 uprising and the city's broader struggle over policing, civil rights, and community relations.
